props.title: Muriel, or the Time of Return
props.initialSlug: A haunting tale of memory's grip.

sections.content: Alain Resnais's **Muriel, or the Time of Return** (1963) revolutionized narrative fragmentation in cinema, building on his earlier experiments in Hiroshima Mon Amour (1959) and Last Year at Marienbad (1961). The film's jarring editing style and discontinuous storytelling perfectly mirror its exploration of trauma, memory, and France's painful colonial legacy in Algeria. Like Chris Marker's La Jetée (1962), Resnais fractures time itself, creating a dizzying portrait of characters haunted by their past while struggling to exist in the present.

sections.content: The film's setting in Boulogne-sur-Mer becomes a character itself, with Resnais capturing the reconstruction of post-war France through its modernizing architecture and shifting social landscape. This approach influenced later New Wave films like Jean-Luc Godard's **2 or 3 Things I Know About Her** (1967) and Jacques Tati's **Playtime** (1967), which similarly used urban spaces to comment on France's rapid modernization and loss of historical memory.

Delphine Seyrig's performance as Hélène anchors the film's complex temporal structure. Her attempts to reconnect with an old lover mirror France's inability to reconcile with its colonial past, particularly the Algerian War. This theme of national trauma would later be explored in Michael Haneke's Hidden (2005) and Claire Denis's White Material (2009), both examining colonial guilt through similarly fragmented narratives. sections.content: Resnais's revolutionary editing techniques in **Muriel** created a new cinematic grammar for depicting memory and trauma. The film's influence can be seen in later works like Nicolas Roeg's **Don't Look Now** (1973) and Atom Egoyan's **The Sweet Hereafter** (1997), which similarly use fractured narratives to explore grief and collective trauma.
